newsitem.title: USA: Dead men don't talk in Texas, but do they vote?.
newsitem.headline: Dead men don't talk in Texas, but do they vote?.

text.p: Dead men don't talk, and Texas election officials are taking steps to make sure they don't vote, either.

Texas Secretary of State Tony Garza called on election officials to review lists of more than 10 million registered voters statewide after a random audit found the names of 7,600 dead people on the voting rolls of four Texas counties.
In a letter sent to elections officials this week, Garza said the names of 6,000 dead people were listed among the 760,428 registered voters in Bexar County in south Texas.
Bexar County Tax Assessor Sylvia Romo, who is responsible for the county's voter rolls, said Friday there was no evidence of voter fraud.
"To my knowledge there have been no fraudulent voting activities in Bexar County as a result of deceased persons' names being on the voter registration rolls," she said in a letter to Garza.
The random audit was triggered by complaints from San Antonio-area voters who complained about seeing the names of dead relatives on Bexar County registration lists during last year's elections.
In Harris County, elections officials last year removed the names of about 6,000 of the 1.66 million voters in the Houston-area after reviewing lists of deceased residents.

"Most names are removed as relatives point out deceased names, but we do it routinely because the Secretarty of State furnishes the tape to us," said Jack Grace, a county clerk. "It's a thing we continually work on."
